segments.name: The Kentucky Boyhood: Stringtown on the Pike

stops.name: West Bloomfield, the surveyor's son
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia and the nkyviews long biography agree on 19 April 1849 and on both parents' names. Coordinate corrected here to the OpenStreetMap position of the Town of West Bloomfield, Ontario County; the value carried in the research dossier sat about four kilometres too far east.
stops.campa: In West Bloomfield, Ontario County, New York, a son is born to Nelson Marvin Lloyd and Sophia Webster Lloyd. Both parents teach school; the father also surveys, and it is the surveying that will move the household off this ground within four years. They name the boy John Uri. He will keep no memory of the state at all, and will spell that middle name out in full on the title page of every book he writes, chemistry manuals and Kentucky novels alike.
suggested_refs: The town of West Bloomfield, Ontario County, New York, the only northern ground in his life

stops.name: Burlington, the family comes south
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the move and its cause by the Lloyd Library finding aid and nkyviews; the month is unrecorded and defaults to January. Coordinate corrected to the OpenStreetMap position of Burlington, Boone County, about two kilometres from the dossier value.
stops.campa: Nelson Lloyd takes work surveying a proposed railroad from Covington to Louisville, and the family comes south into Boone County, Kentucky, settling near Burlington. The Ohio River runs a few miles to the north. On the far bank stands Cincinnati, the largest manufacturing city in the West, its slaughterhouses and its drug houses both. The boy is four. Everything he will make is on that side of the water and nearly everything he will write about is on this one.

stops.name: Petersburg, the last survivor of Perry's victory
stops.date_confidence: the Petersburg residence in the 1850s is attested by nkyviews; the year here only orders the segment. The two John Norris manuscripts are attested but undated: finding aid Series XIX, Box 40, Folders 578 and 579. Coordinate corrected to OpenStreetMap; the dossier value fell some ten kilometres south.
stops.campa: The parents look for teaching work and the household moves again, downriver to Petersburg, a landing town that had been Norman's Mill in Normansville before it was renamed. Here the boy learns the local trade of listening to old men. John Norris of Petersburg is pointed out to him as the last survivor of Perry's victory on Lake Erie, a battle already half a century gone. Sixty years later Lloyd will file two manuscripts about Norris, one of them nothing but the old man's recollections of the War of 1812, taken down and kept.

stops.name: Florence, the boy on the pike
stops.date_confidence: Florence as the settled family home c. 1854-1863 is attested by the Boone County history bio; the year here orders the segment. The Fort Mitchell reminiscence 'Old Fort Mitchell On The Height' is attested but undated: finding aid Series XIX, Box 40, Folder 587.
stops.campa: Florence is a single string of houses strung along the turnpike, which is why the country calls it Stringtown on the pike. He will not have to invent that name. This is the settled home, the ground of the boyhood: the road, the store, the church, the talk of everyone on it. In the war years he watches troops move through a county that sends men both ways, and hears of the earthworks going up at Fort Mitchell on the height to the east, which he sets down as an old man under the title 'Old Fort Mitchell On The Height.'

stops.name: Big Bone Lick, the salt marsh full of mammoths
stops.date_confidence: the two essays are attested in the finding aid (Box 43, Folder 760 and Box 39, Folder 551) but carry no date, and no source records a boyhood visit; the year is an ordering device only. Coordinate corrected to the OpenStreetMap position of Big Bone Lick State Park.
stops.campa: Ten miles southwest of Florence the ground gives out into a marsh of sulfur and salt springs where the bones of mammoth and mastodon came up out of the mud by the wagonload, shipped east and to Paris while the republic was young. The boy grows up within a morning's walk of the largest bone bed of extinct animals in North America. He will write it twice, as 'Man and Mammoth At Big Bone Lick, Kentucky' and as 'The Big Bone Country of Kentucky.' The water still smells of sulfur.
suggested_refs: Lloyd's essays 'Man and Mammoth At Big Bone Lick, Kentucky' and 'The Big Bone Country of Kentucky'

stops.name: East Third Street, the attic room
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The apprenticeship to William J. M. Gordon is attested by the finding aid and Wikipedia, but the sources give 1863 or 1864 for the crossing and the discrepancy is not resolved here; the boarding-house attic on East Third Street rests on nkyviews alone. Flannery's chronology and Lloyd's first diary, cited in the research dossier for 1864, were not reachable.
stops.campa: At about fourteen he crosses the Ohio and takes an attic room in a cheap boarding house on East Third Street, apprenticed to the pharmacist William J. M. Gordon. The terms are the terms of the trade: sweeping, washing bottles, watching, and after a while grinding and weighing. There is no schooling in it beyond what a master chooses to explain. Whether he crossed in 1863 or in 1864 the sources do not agree, and neither Flannery's chronology nor Lloyd's own first diary could be opened to settle it. His formal education ends here, in this attic, at fourteen.
suggested_refs: The boarding houses of East Third Street, Cincinnati, in the last year of the war

stops.name: Eger's pharmacy, the apprenticeship notebook
stops.date_confidence: attested, and upgraded from the dossier's tradition: finding aid Series VIII, Box 14, Folder 295, 'John Uri Lloyd's apprenticeship notebook with George Eger, 1866,' with the Laboratory Notebooks series running 1866-1917. nkyviews adds that Eger was a second two-year term after Gordon, both finished by about 1867. Eger's street address is in no reachable source, so this coordinate is a downtown approximation.
stops.campa: After Gordon he is bound a second time, to George Eger, trained in Germany, and the German laboratory habit takes: weigh it, record it, date the page. He is seventeen, and both apprenticeships are done by about his eighteenth year, with no diploma at the end of either. The notebook he keeps in Eger's shop survives in a box on Court Street, first of a run of laboratory notebooks that does not stop until 1917. Where Eger's shop stood is in no source anyone has reached.

stops.name: Gordon's pharmacy, the article of agreement
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Article of Agreement is finding aid Series XI, Box 18, Folder 351, dated 25 March 1870. The shop's exact address is not given in any reachable source and the coordinate is a downtown approximation.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of March he signs an Article of Agreement with his first master, buying Gordon's chemical apparatus outright: retorts, balances, flasks, the working glass of a trade passing across a table from the man who taught it to the boy who once swept for him. He is not yet twenty-one. The paper survives in the family archive, filed among the legal documents rather than the reminiscences: Series XI, Box 18, Folder 351, an Article of Agreement between W. J. M. Gordon and John Uri Lloyd.

stops.name: H. M. Merrell and Company, the Eclectic laboratory
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1871 and for the firm by nkyviews and the Lloyd papers biographical note. The tradition that John King and John Milton Scudder brokered the appointment, and that Lloyd was 'laboratory manager,' is attested in no reachable source and is not carried here; King appears in the finding aid only as a correspondent, Box 9, Folder 168.
stops.campa: H. M. Merrell and Company is the principal Cincinnati house supplying the Eclectic physicians, the American school that prescribes native plants where the regular schools prescribe mercury and the lancet. Lloyd takes the laboratory at twenty-two and sets himself the problem that will hold him for sixty years: a plant is not a chemical. No two lots of goldenseal root assay alike, no two seasons, no two hillsides. How does a house sell a physician a dose it cannot promise twice?
suggested_refs: The Eclectic materia medica of the 1870s: hydrastis, podophyllum, echinacea, and the problem of standardizing them

stops.name: Cincinnati, the marriage to Adaline Meader
stops.date_confidence: December 1876 is attested by nkyviews. The day is not: the 27th given in the research dossier is unsupported, while nkyviews's 'ten days after marriage' before her death on 7 January 1877 would imply the 28th. Month kept, day dropped.
stops.campa: He marries Adaline Meader, a Cincinnati schoolteacher, in the last days of December. He is twenty-seven and has been five years at Merrell's bench. Addie is what the archive calls her. That summer the Centennial Exposition at Philadelphia had stood open six months at Fairmount Park, showing the country its own manufactures, the drug houses among them. Nothing of the courtship is recorded anywhere that survives. The day of the wedding is not recorded either, only the month.
suggested_refs: The Adaline Meader Lloyd papers, Series IV, Box 2, Folders 33-34 of the Lloyd family archive

stops.name: New York, the ten-day marriage
stops.date_confidence: the death date of 7 January 1877 and the cause, acute peritonitis, are attested by nkyviews, and the finding aid dates the Addie Meader Lloyd material to 1877. The New York honeymoon is tradition only, attested by no reachable source; the record does not name the city, and this coordinate stands in for a place it does not give.
stops.campa: Ten days into the marriage Adaline dies of acute peritonitis, on the seventh of January, on a wedding journey the record does not locate. The Lloyd papers keep her in two folders: an obituary, a funeral bulletin, portraits, and a lock of hair. He is twenty-seven and a widower, and he goes back to the laboratory. He will not marry again for three and a half years. The folders stay in the family's own archive for a century and are numbered there still.

stops.name: Boone County, the marriage to Emma Rouse
stops.date_confidence: 1880 is attested only as an approximation, nkyviews giving 'approximately 1880, three and a half years after Adaline's death.' The 10 June sometimes printed appears in no reachable source; month and day default. The finding aid's 'Emma Rouse Lloyd, 1868-1900' correspondence, Box 6, Folder 58, is consistent with the childhood acquaintance but does not prove it.
stops.campa: Three and a half years a widower, he marries Emma V. Rouse of Boone County, daughter of Thomas Rouse, whom the accounts call a friend from childhood; letters between them in the family archive run back to 1868, when he was nineteen and still bound apprentice. The chemist who crossed the river at fourteen marries back into the county that raised him. The wedding day itself is nowhere in the record, only the year, and they will be married fifty-two years.
suggested_refs: The Emma Rouse Lloyd correspondence, 1868-1900, Box 6, Folder 58 of the Lloyd papers

stops.name: 2604 Harris Avenue, Norwood: the city of the future
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Norwood Ohio Historical Society gives the address, the arrival about 1882, and the renaming of the cross street, and the advocacy is independently corroborated by essay titles in the Lloyd papers. Coordinate corrected to the OpenStreetMap position of 2604 Harris Avenue, about two kilometres from the dossier value.
stops.campa: He settles Emma at 2604 Harris Avenue in Norwood, on the highlands above Cincinnati, and takes up the village as a cause. He is thirty-three and the subject is water pressure. The cross street beside his own is renamed Lloyd Avenue while he is still living on it. He argues natural gas into the columns of the Norwood Gazette, addresses the taxpayers and water consumers of the place directly and in print, and writes the pamphlets 'Norwood, Gem of the Highlands' and 'Norwood's Opportunity.'
suggested_refs: Lloyd's Norwood pamphlets: 'Norwood, Gem of the Highlands,' 'Norwood's Opportunity,' 'To The Taxpayers and Water Consumers of Norwood,' and 'Natural Gas for Norwood'

stops.name: Cincinnati, the name on the door becomes Lloyd Brothers
stops.date_confidence: the 1886 date and the name Lloyd Brothers, Pharmacists are attested by Wikipedia and the Lloyd Library finding aid, but the mechanism is told differently by every account: Wikipedia has the brothers purchasing Merrell and Thorpe, the finding aid credits John and Nelson Ashley, and the dossier's version, Curtis replacing Abner Thorp, is attested nowhere. The intermediate steps of 1877 and 1881 are company tradition only.
stops.campa: The firm changes its name three times in nine years as the Lloyds buy their way through it: Merrell, Thorp and Lloyd, then Thorp and Lloyd Brothers, then simply Lloyd Brothers, Pharmacists. Three brothers divide it cleanly. Nelson Ashley keeps the books, Curtis Gates takes the plants and, increasingly, the fungi, and John takes the chemistry and the line of Specific Medicines the house is built on. Who bought out whom, and in what order, is told differently by every surviving account.

stops.name: The Eclectic Medical Institute, the chemistry of the botanical dissent
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing, and the dossier's tag downgraded. No reachable source dates the professorship to 1878: nkyviews says only that he taught there 'for many years' and was president 1896-1904, and the Lloyd papers biographical note says only that he taught chemistry at the Eclectic Medical College. The 1878 here orders the segment and is not itself attested; the dossier's further claim of an 1895 versus 1907 end-year dispute is unsupported too.
stops.campa: The Eclectic Medical Institute is the college of the botanical dissent, the school that answered heroic bleeding and calomel with American plants. Lloyd teaches chemistry and pharmacy there, and serves as its president from 1896 to 1904. He has never sat in a college classroom as a student in his life. The Institute's chemistry is his chemistry: the men in that lecture room will prescribe what the men in his laboratory make. What year he began teaching there no reachable source says.
suggested_refs: The Eclectic Medical Institute of Cincinnati, the last major school of American botanical medicine
sources: nkyviews.com, long biography of John Uri Lloyd

stops.name: The Cincinnati College of Pharmacy, professor of chemistry
stops.date_confidence: 1882-1887 is attested by nkyviews and is used here; other accounts give 1883-1887 and the start year is not resolved. The first Ebert Prize in 1882 and the presidency of the American Pharmaceutical Association in 1887 are reconstruction only: no award record or association minute was reachable.
stops.campa: For five sessions he is professor of chemistry at the Cincinnati College of Pharmacy as well, lecturing to young men who will take home the diploma he does not hold. In the same decade the American Pharmaceutical Association gives him its Ebert Prize for research and then elects him its president. The national profession has taken the Eclectics' chemist for its own, eighteen years after the attic on East Third Street. Neither the award record nor the association's minute could be found; both honours rest here on biographical tradition alone.
suggested_refs: The Ebert Prize of the American Pharmaceutical Association and its 1887 presidency, both claimed for Lloyd by biographical tradition

stops.name: Cincinnati, the famous Hydrastis controversy
stops.date_confidence: attested, and upgraded from the dossier's tradition: finding aid Series II, Box 2, Folder 15, 'The Famous Hydrastis Controversy, 1888-1889,' an autobiographical composition by Lloyd himself, so the span is two years rather than the single year 1888. The later Treasury fight of 1898-1900 is attested at Series XII, Box 18.
stops.campa: Hydrastis canadensis, goldenseal, is the plant the whole Eclectic pharmacopoeia turns on, and the fight over it runs two years: what its alkaloids are, whose preparation holds them, who had them first. Lloyd is at the centre of it. Long afterward he writes the episode up himself and files it among his own papers as autobiography, under the title 'The Famous Hydrastis Controversy.' The adjective is his. Ten years on he is fighting the Treasury instead, over a war tax laid on proprietary medicines.
suggested_refs: Lloyd's autobiographical file 'The Famous Hydrastis Controversy, 1888-1889'

segments.name: Etidorhpa, the Manuscript Held Thirty Years

stops.name: Cincinnati, Elixirs and Flavoring Extracts
stops.date_confidence: attested by Wikipedia's bibliography of Lloyd; month and day unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Elixirs and Flavoring Extracts: Their History, Formulae, and Methods of Preparation goes out under his name, a working book for working druggists, formula after formula with the history of each one attached to it. Twenty years at the bench are in it: what a preparation is, where it came from, why the last batch failed. In three years the same hand will publish an account of a man taken underground by a stranger who gives no name. For now he is forty-three, and this is the first substantial book he has written.

stops.name: Cincinnati, the Author's Edition of Etidorhpa
stops.date_confidence: attested, with two corrections to the dossier. The 1895 printing names J. U. Lloyd himself as publisher, Cincinnati, with presswork and binding by Cranston and Curts (Internet Archive metadata for etidorhpaorend00lloy), not the Robert Clarke Company; and the often repeated figure of more than 1,200 subscribers appears in no reachable source. The archive does hold the prospectus, edition announcement and order forms, Box 28, Folder 401.
stops.campa: He publishes it himself. Etidorhpa, or The End of Earth, a signed Author's Edition out of Cincinnati, the presswork and binding by Cranston and Curts, the plates by J. Augustus Knapp: the blind guide, the fungus forest, the cavern of unrest. The title is Aphrodite spelled backward. Subscribers order it by prospectus and printed form. Lloyd's preface presents the whole book as a manuscript handed to him by another man, under conditions he says he is bound to keep.
stops.quote: the manuscript of this book has been in my possession for a period of seven years, and my lips must now be sealed concerning all that transpired in connection therewith outside the subject-matter recorded

stops.name: The Ohio Valley, a November night in Drury's library
stops.date_confidence: the novel's own geography, not a journey Lloyd made. Etidorhpa's frame opens in a library in the Ohio Valley in November, and is pinned here at Lloyd's own Cincinnati; the February date orders it after the book's publication stop and means nothing else. Text verified verbatim against Project Gutenberg #37775, Chapter I.
stops.campa: The book begins where the man writing it lives. Llewellyn Drury sits alone among old books on a November night in the Ohio Valley, a month Lloyd calls one of possibilities, and stakes everything he owns, his soul included, on being alone in the room. A visitor is already there: a man with a forehead so vast it is nearly a deformity, who gives no name and signs himself I-Am-The-Man-Who-Did-It. He asks Drury to take down his account and bury it thirty years before printing it.
stops.quote: You have lost your wager; you are not alone.
stops.quote_source: John Uri Lloyd, Etidorhpa (1895), Chapter I, Project Gutenberg #37775

stops.name: Biswell's Hill, Kentucky: the mouth of the descent
stops.date_confidence: fictional geography with a declared stand-in coordinate. The novel's front matter names a cavern discovered at Biswell's Hill and 'The Punch Bowls and Caverns of Kentucky'; the Public Domain Review says only that the entrance is to be found in Kentucky. No source identifies a real cave, and the coordinate used here is Mammoth Cave, a substitution the sources do not make. No reachable source shows Lloyd citing or naming Symmes; that connection is doctrinal, not documented.
stops.campa: The narrator is led blindfolded through a Kentucky cave mouth and down, past the last daylight, into a hollow earth of fungus forests, a windless sea, and gravity thinning as the crust is left above. It is the doctrine John Cleves Symmes Jr. preached from Cincinnati platforms in 1820, turning a wooden globe with the poles cut open, now fitted out with a novelist's furniture: instruments, arguments, and a guide who eats nothing and does not age. Lloyd never says which cave. Kentucky has a great many.

stops.name: The Robert Clarke Company, the sixth edition
stops.date_confidence: attested: Project Gutenberg #37775 reproduces the sixth edition, Cincinnati, The Robert Clarke Company, 1896. The quoted review is taken from the 'Some Press Opinions' appendix bound into the book itself, pp. 385-386, under the heading 'The Inter-Ocean, Chicago'; the 1895 newspaper page itself could not be located, Chronicling America returning no match, so the wording rests on the book's own reprinting.
stops.campa: Within a year the private book has become a trade book: a revised sixth edition from the Robert Clarke Company of Cincinnati, sold to anyone who asks. The reviews are bewildered in the way that sells copies, and the volume carries a sheaf of them bound in at the back under the heading 'Some Press Opinions.' Lloyd, a manufacturing chemist with a laboratory to run, answers his correspondence, letter by letter. Is the manuscript genuine? Has the author been underground himself?
stops.quote: For eighteen years the writer has been seated at his desk, and all kinds of books have been passed in review, but has never before met with such a stumper as Etidorhpa. Its name is a stunner, and its title-page, head-lines, and weird, artistic pictures send you such a ghastly welcome as to make goblins on the walls, and fill the close room with spooks and mystery.
stops.quote_source: The Inter-Ocean, Chicago, 1895, as reprinted in the 'Some Press Opinions' appendix to Etidorhpa, Project Gutenberg #37775, pp. 385-386

stops.name: Mount Rainier, the right side of the car
stops.date_confidence: The Right Side of the Car: A Story of the Northern Pacific Railway is attested to 1897 by Wikipedia. The Lloyd papers keep Mount Rainier as a subject file of its own, Series XVIII, Box 45, Folder 695, but do not date the trip, so pinning the 1897 story to the mountain is an inference stated as such.
stops.campa: He rides the Northern Pacific across the northern tier and writes The Right Side of the Car, a story that turns on which side of a railway carriage a passenger happens to be sitting on, and therefore on what she sees out of the window. The mountain is the thing to be seen. In his papers Mount Rainier is kept as a subject file of its own, Series XVIII, Box 45, Folder 695, with no date written on it anywhere. Nothing in the archive says when he made the trip.

stops.name: Florence, Stringtown on the Pike
stops.date_confidence: 1900 is attested four times over, by Open Library, by Internet Archive's Dodd, Mead record, by Kentucky Historical Marker #2540, and by the Boone County history bio. Wikipedia's 1901 is wrong and is not followed. The finding aid also holds Scrapbook Volume 10, 'Book reviews of John Uri Lloyd novel Stringtown on the Pike 1900-1901.'
stops.campa: Stringtown on the Pike takes the boyhood ground and puts it in print: the turnpike, the dialect, the feuds, a poisoning and a trial, and a border county that sent its men both ways in the war. Florence gets its second name back out of the book, and keeps it. It is the most successful thing he writes; the reviews fill a whole scrapbook volume, running from 1900 into 1901. He is fifty-one, and has published in one decade a hollow-earth romance and a Kentucky dialect novel from the same desk.

stops.name: The knobs of Kentucky, Warwick of the Knobs
stops.date_confidence: the 1901 publication is attested by Wikipedia. The report that Grover Cleveland read the novel, corresponded with Lloyd from 1901 to 1907 and fished with him comes from the research dossier's characterization of the family archive and was confirmed in no reachable source; it is carried here as tradition and named as such in the campa.
stops.campa: Warwick of the Knobs follows, set in the hill country of hard-shell preaching and family judgment. He is a novelist with a list now, and the list is Kentucky. Grover Cleveland, out of office, is said to have read the book, to have written to Lloyd for years afterward and to have fished with him. That friendship is reported in the family's own tradition and confirmed nowhere else; the letters, if they exist, are in no catalogue that has been reached.

stops.name: Constantinople, the college and the drug bazaar
stops.date_confidence: attested by the finding aid, Series XIII, Box 19, Folder 375, for the American College for Girls material and the consular introductions of the 1906 journey; the month is unrecorded. The essay 'Turkish Drugs' is attested at Box 43, Folder 668 but carries no place more precise than the Ottoman Empire.
stops.campa: At fifty-seven he sails for the Ottoman Empire carrying consular introductions. In Constantinople he gathers material on the American College for Girls, the missionary school above the Bosphorus, and files it with the addresses of everyone he has met. He also does what a pharmacist does in a strange market: he walks the drug bazaar and writes down what is sold in it. The note goes into the archive as 'Turkish Drugs,' Box 43, Folder 668, with no place on it more precise than the empire.

stops.name: Galata, the whirling dervishes
stops.date_confidence: the essay 'The Whirling Dervishes' is attested verbatim in the finding aid, Series XIX, Box 41, Folder 610. The venue is not: nothing in the finding aid names the Galata Mevlevihanesi or any other tekke, so this coordinate is a researcher's inference and the stop is attested as to the writing, reconstruction as to the place. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He watches the sema: the ney and the drum, the white skirts opening, the right hand turned up and the left hand turned down, an hour of it, and the men neither dizzy nor exalted at the end but simply finished. He writes it up as 'The Whirling Dervishes,' four pages in a life otherwise given to formulae. Which lodge admitted him nobody wrote down. The Mevlevi houses of the city took foreign visitors that year, and the tekke at Galata was the one to which foreigners were usually taken.
suggested_refs: Lloyd's essay 'The Whirling Dervishes', Series XIX, Box 41, Folder 610
The Galata Mevlevihanesi, the Mevlevi lodge most often shown to foreign visitors in 1906

stops.name: Smyrna, the correspondent on the quay
stops.date_confidence: attested: the finding aid holds correspondence with Ahmed Ramsay and miscellaneous Smyrna addresses from the journey, Series XIII, Box 19, Folders 362 and 364, with the correspondence running 1906-1911. The visit itself is placed in 1906 and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Smyrna is the great outlet of the Anatolian gum and drug trade, opium and scammony and tragacanth moving out through it, and the man taking notes on the quay sells alkaloids for a living. Here he acquires the thing he acquires everywhere, which is a correspondent. Ahmed Ramsay's letters and a sheaf of Smyrna addresses travel home in his baggage, and the port stays joined to Court Street by mail long after the ship has gone. The last of those letters is dated 1911.
suggested_refs: The Ahmed Ramsay correspondence and Smyrna addresses, Series XIII, Box 19, Folders 362 and 364

stops.name: Ephesus, the ruins written twice
stops.date_confidence: attested as writings: the finding aid holds both 'Ephesus' (Series XIX, Box 39, Folder 561) and 'The Ruins of Ephesus' (Box 40, Folder 592). Neither is dated, and the month here only places the stop within the 1906 voyage.
stops.campa: He walks the ruins of Ephesus: the marble street, the broken face of the library of Celsus, the theatre where a crowd once shouted for two hours together. A man who has spent thirty years insisting that a preparation be traced to its source is standing in a city whose sources are all in dispute. He writes the place twice, a short piece and a long one, 'Ephesus' and 'The Ruins of Ephesus,' neither of them dated by the archive. The harbour that made the city rich silted up sixteen centuries ago, and the sea now lies three miles off across flat ground.
suggested_refs: Lloyd's two Ephesus manuscripts, Box 39, Folder 561 and Box 40, Folder 592
sources: Lloyd Library and Museum, John Uri Lloyd Papers finding aid, Series XIX, Box 39, Folder 561 and Box 40, Folder 592

stops.name: Rhodes, the home of mastic
stops.date_confidence: the finding aid names the island: Box 40, Folder 573 is titled 'The Island of Rhodes / Home of Mastic,' with 'Mastic and Its Oriental Uses, A Letter From The Orient' in Boxes 53-54 and 'Mastiche notes and recipe' at Box 42, Folder 643. The research dossier placed this on Chios because mastic is historically a Chios crop; nothing attests that Lloyd went to Chios, and the discrepancy is stated in the campa rather than resolved.
stops.campa: On Rhodes he goes after mastic, the resin that is chewed, distilled, varnished with and dosed with, and comes away with a recipe and the makings of two essays, 'Mastic and Its Oriental Uses' and 'Home of Mastic.' This is what his travelling is for. Other men go to look at ruins; he goes where a drug comes out of a tree and asks who cuts it, in what month, and into what vessel. The mastic itself has always been grown on Chios, one island north of where he stands.

stops.name: Aden, the water tanks in the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested as a writing: 'The Water Tanks of Aden Were A Surprise,' finding aid Series XIX, Box 41, Folder 609. The call at Aden is placed within the 1906 voyage and the month orders the segment; no source dates the visit itself.
stops.campa: The ship calls at Aden and he climbs to the tanks: a stair of cisterns cut into volcanic rock above the town, ancient, of uncertain date, built to hold the rain of a place that hardly gets any. Forty years in the trade of holding liquids in vessels, and what stops him is a hillside of empty stone basins. He writes it up under a title that keeps the surprise in it, 'The Water Tanks of Aden Were A Surprise,' and files it at Box 41, Folder 609, with no date on the visit itself.
suggested_refs: The Tawila Tanks of Aden and Lloyd's essay upon them

stops.name: Loreto, the mission on the Sea of Cortez
stops.date_confidence: attested as writings, undated as travel: 'Journey to the Sea of Cortez' is Series II, Box 2, Folder 18, filed with Lloyd's own life papers, and 'My Visit To Loreto' is Series XIX, Box 41, Folder 605. The research dossier cited the latter at Box 54, Folder 750, which is the index entry in the alphabetical article list, not the manuscript. The year 1908 is an ordering device and is attested by nothing.
stops.campa: He goes down the Sea of Cortez to Loreto in Baja California, the first mission of the Californias, its stone church standing over a town the capital moved away from a century before. The desert around it grows the pharmacopoeia of another continent: damiana, jatropha, elephant tree. Two manuscripts come of the trip, an autobiographical account he calls 'Journey to the Sea of Cortez,' filed with his own life papers, and a shorter essay, 'My Visit To Loreto.' Neither carries a date anywhere in the archive.

stops.name: Canyon de Chelly, the Navajo medicine man
stops.date_confidence: attested as a writing, undated as travel: 'Experience in Canon de Chelly with a Navajo Medicine Man,' Series XIX, Box 39, Folder 563, with 'Six descriptions of Arizona for Judge Thompson' at Box 39, Folder 555 and 'A Jaunt Through the Land of the Navajos and Moquis' at Box 40, Folder 574. Judge Albert C. Thompson is confirmed as a correspondent, Box 13, Folder 265, 1906. The year here orders the segment. Coordinate corrected to the OpenStreetMap position of the canyon; the dossier value fell some nine kilometres outside it. The dossier's separate cliff-dwelling stop is folded in here because its location was an admitted substitution.
stops.campa: In the canyon he meets a Navajo medicine man and writes the encounter down as 'Experience in Canon de Chelly with a Navajo Medicine Man.' He is sixty, a professor of chemistry, a manufacturer of standardized plant preparations, sitting with a practitioner of a pharmacopoeia his own profession keeps no register for. He tours the cliff dwellings too, and the Hopi country the period called Moqui, and sends six written descriptions of Arizona back east to Judge Albert C. Thompson, who is one of his correspondents.

stops.name: 3901 Clifton Avenue, the Romanesque house
stops.date_confidence: attested by the National Park Service record for 'Lloyd, John Uri, House': 3901 Clifton Avenue, Cincinnati, architect James W. McLaughlin, Romanesque, structure completed 1890, NRHP reference 73001461, listed 7 March 1973. The dossier's 'built 1888-1890' is not the NPS wording. Coordinate corrected to OpenStreetMap; the dossier value sat about two kilometres off.
stops.campa: The house on Clifton Avenue is finished: Romanesque, heavy stone, round arches, by James W. McLaughlin, the architect Cincinnati used for its hospitals and its public library. Lloyd is forty-one and the firm is prospering. What the house makes plain is the problem coming: his own chemical and pharmaceutical literature is stacked on one side, Curtis's botany and mycology on the other, and both collections are still growing faster than any private house can hold them.

stops.name: West Court Street, the books take a building
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Lloyd Library's own history: acquisition of 224 West Court Street from 1902, a separate library building at 309 West Court Street in 1907, expanded by fifty feet in 1912. A contradiction is left open: the research dossier describes the 309 building as arising earlier and merely being expanded in 1912, and dates the firm's presence at that address to the 1890s, which cannot hold if the building went up in 1907. Coordinate corrected to OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: First the brothers buy the building at 224 West Court Street to put the two collections under one roof; then the collections take that too, and a separate library building goes up at 309, and in 1912 it is lengthened by fifty feet. What began as a working shelf beside a laboratory has become an institution with a reading room. The Lloyds keep buying: herbals, pharmacopoeias, travel, mycology, the whole literature of what plants are and what they do to people.
stops.quote: Each volume adds to the oppression, each old tome casts the influence of its spirit over the beholder, for have not these old books spirits?
stops.quote_source: John Uri Lloyd, Etidorhpa; or, The End of Earth (1895), Preface, Project Gutenberg #37775

stops.name: Cincinnati, the histories of the vegetable drugs
stops.date_confidence: attested by Wikipedia's bibliography: Life and Medical Discoveries of Samuel Thomson (1909), The Eclectic Alkaloids, Resins, Resinoids, Oleo-Resins and Concentrated Principles (1910), History of the Vegetable Drugs of the Pharmacopoeia of the United States (1911). The stop is dated to the last of the three; months and days are unrecorded.
stops.campa: In three years he writes the history of his own tradition three times over. Life and Medical Discoveries of Samuel Thomson reconstructs, out of pamphlets and almanacs and the records of the trials, the New Hampshire root doctor who patented a system of botanic medicine and sold family rights to it door to door. The chemist is now the archivist of the herbalists his firm descends from. Then The Eclectic Alkaloids in 1910, and in 1911 the History of the Vegetable Drugs of the Pharmacopoeia of the United States.
suggested_refs: Life and Medical Discoveries of Samuel Thomson (1909), Lloyd's reconstruction of Thomsonian medicine from the early literature
sources: Wikipedia, 'John Uri Lloyd'

stops.name: Cincinnati, Lloyd's reagent
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The patent number US 1,048,712 for the extraction and purification of alkaloids with aluminium silicate, filed 23 February 1912 and granted 31 December 1912, is carried from the research dossier's patent table; the USPTO record itself was not pulled in this pass and no second source was reached.
stops.campa: Lloyd's reagent is hydrated aluminium silicate, and what it does is hold alkaloids out of solution and then give them back. No heat, no alcohol tearing the rest of the plant apart, none of the loss the older methods took for granted. He and the firm file in February and the patent, number 1,048,712, is granted on the last day of the year. Analytical laboratories will still be running alkaloid work on the reagent long after the Specific Medicines go off the market. The patent file itself has not been opened here; the number comes from a secondary table.
suggested_refs: United States patent 1,048,712, aluminium silicate for the extraction, purification and exclusion of alkaloids
sources: Research dossier patent table, flagged as unverified against the USPTO record

segments.name: The Last of the Three Brothers

stops.name: 309 West Court Street, the library made public by deed
stops.date_confidence: attested: Curtis Gates Lloyd established a trust for the library in 1917 (National Library of Medicine finding-aid content on the Lloyd family papers), and the three brothers a broader trust arrangement for public access in 1919 (Wikipedia). The collection figure of about fifty thousand volumes is given by the Lloyd Library as a mid-1920s approximation, not a dated count.
stops.campa: Curtis settles a trust on the library in 1917, and two years later the three brothers together put the whole arrangement on a footing that will outlive them: an endowment, a board, and the rule that anyone at all may come in and read. It is not a bequest waiting on their deaths; they sign it while all three are alive and running a business next door to the reading room. By the middle of the following decade the shelves hold some fifty thousand volumes and a reading room open to anybody in Cincinnati.
suggested_refs: The Lloyd brothers' trust deeds of 1917 and 1919, which made the library a public institution during their lifetimes

stops.name: Cincinnati, the last of the three brothers
stops.date_confidence: 1926 for Curtis Gates Lloyd's death is attested twice, by the Lloyd Library history, which gives his dates as 1859-1926, and by the related accession 'Curtis Gates Lloyd Papers 1859-1926.' The day of 11 November given in the research dossier appears in neither and is not carried. Nelson Ashley Lloyd's death in 1925 is family tradition only.
stops.campa: Nelson Ashley goes first, then Curtis, and John is the last of the three. Curtis leaves a mycological herbarium of tens of thousands of specimens and a reputation for publishing his opinions of rival mycologists without softening them. The firm is still Lloyd Brothers and there is one brother. The library made out of the two of them, the chemist's shelf and the botanist's, now belongs to a trust and to anyone who walks in off Court Street. He is seventy-seven and keeps working.

stops.name: Cincinnati, Felix Moses of Stringtown
stops.date_confidence: attested by Wikipedia: a signed Author's Edition of 500 copies with J. Augustus Knapp illustrations, based on a real Boone County, Kentucky Jewish peddler. Month and day unrecorded.
stops.campa: At eighty-one he brings out one more novel, five hundred signed copies, Knapp illustrating again: Felix Moses, the Beloved Jew of Stringtown on the Pike. Felix Moses was a real peddler who walked the Boone County roads with a pack when Lloyd was a boy on the pike, sixty-six years before. The book is written from the boy's side of the transaction: the child at the edge of the road, watching the stranger everyone in the county trades with and talks about once he has gone on.

stops.name: Cincinnati, the death of Emma Rouse Lloyd
stops.date_confidence: 1932 is attested by the archive's related accession, 'Emma Rouse Lloyd Papers 1858-1932.' The day of 27 November given in the research dossier is unattested in any reachable source; month and day are therefore defaulted rather than printed as fact.
stops.campa: Emma Rouse Lloyd dies, fifty-two years married to him, and her papers are kept as their own accession in the library her husband and his brothers built, running back to 1858, when she was a girl in Boone County and he was a boy four miles off. The archive is the family habit by now: the wife's letters, the first wife's funeral bulletin, the brothers' herbarium sheets, the apprenticeship notebook of 1866, all of it numbered and shelved in the same building. He is eighty-three.

stops.name: Cincinnati, the dinner for Einstein
stops.date_confidence: attested as a dated event with its own file in the Lloyd papers, Series XVIII, Box 45, Folder 686. The venue is not named in the finding aid, and no reachable source establishes whether Albert Einstein was present at it or whether the two men ever met.
stops.campa: Cincinnati gives a dinner in honour of Albert Einstein and Lloyd goes to it, at eighty-three, and keeps the paper from the evening. That paper is the only reason the evening exists at all: a dated folder in his own archive, no venue written on it, no note of who spoke. That spring Einstein is leaving Germany and will not return. Whether the guest of honour was in the room, and whether the two men ever stood in the same one, the folder does not say.

stops.name: Van Nuys, death at his daughter's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia and ExploreKYHistory both give death of pneumonia on 9 April 1936 at the Van Nuys home of his daughter Anna Lloyd Welbourn, ten days short of his eighty-seventh birthday. One source, lloydhouse.com, misdates the death to 1938, against every other source checked.
stops.campa: He goes west to visit his daughter Anna Lloyd Welbourn in Van Nuys, and there in the spring he takes pneumonia and dies of it, ten days short of his eighty-seventh birthday. He crossed the Ohio at fourteen and lived in one city from that day; the last of all his travelling turns out to have been a visit. Two thousand miles from Court Street, the house is a bungalow in a San Fernando Valley town that had been a wheat field when he was already an old man and a famous one.

stops.name: Hopeful Lutheran Church, the ground in Boone County
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Hopeful Lutheran Church Cemetery outside Florence is attested by the Boone County history bio, ExploreKYHistory and a Boone County Public Library History Center item record, but no reachable source gives the date of interment; the day here is a placeholder set after the death. Coordinate corrected to the OpenStreetMap position of the church, about three kilometres west of the value carried in the dossier, which fell in central Florence.
stops.campa: He is cremated in California and the ashes carried back to Boone County, to the ground at Hopeful Lutheran Church outside Florence, where both his wives are buried: Adaline, dead ten days into a marriage in 1877, and Emma, dead after fifty-two years of one. The library on Court Street goes on without him, and in 1970 moves to a purpose-built building on Plum Street with a hundred and fifty thousand volumes in it. In 2019 the state sets a marker in Florence that calls the town Stringtown on the Pike.
